title: Tepotinib for the Treatment of Lung Adenocarcinoma Harboring MET Y1003N Point Mutation: A Case Report
author: Yukihiro Umeda; Satomi Kimura; Junya Kimura; Yoshiaki Imamura; Tamotsu Ishizuka
text:
ABSTRACT
The mesenchymal‐epithelial transition factor (MET) Y1003 mutation, like MET ex14 skipping, is an oncogenic driver mutation that suppresses MET degradation. Herein, we report the case of a 63‐year‐old female patient with lung adenocarcinoma harboring the MET Y1003N mutation, who was treated with tepotinib, a selective type 1b MET tyrosine kinase inhibitor. To the best of our knowledge, no such cases have been reported. The woman was referred to our hospital with the chief complaint of chest pain. After a detailed examination, she was diagnosed with stage IVB lung adenocarcinoma. Next‐generation sequencing revealed an MET Y1003N mutation in the tumor. Tepotinib was administered as the eighth‐line treatment, and the best overall response was a partial response that lasted for 8 months. In lung adenocarcinomas harboring the MET Y1003 mutation, selective type 1b MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors may be an important treatment option, even in heavily pretreated settings.
Keywords: adenocarcinoma of lungs, MET Y1003, mutation, tepotinib, tyrosine kinase inhibitors
This is a unique case of a 63‐year‐old female with lung adenocarcinoma harboring the mesenchymal‐epithelial transition factor (MET) Y1003N mutation, who was treated with tepotinib, a selective type 1b MET tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Although tepotinib treatment was the eighth‐line therapy, the response duration was 8 months. Targeted therapy should be used up front; however, tepotinib may be used in patients harboring the MET Y1003 mutation, even in those with multiple prior treatment regimens.
1. Introduction
The mesenchymal‐epithelial transition factor (MET) protooncogene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase that activates downstream signaling pathways, leading to tumor growth, survival, invasion, and metastasis [1]. Mutations or deletions of exon 14 of the MET gene cause loss of the juxtamembrane domain of the MET, including the c‐Cbl E3 ubiquitin ligase binding site. Consequently, MET ubiquitination is curbed, thereby inhibiting its degradation and triggering MET activation [2]. The Y1003 point mutation in the MET is a functional analogue of MET ex14 skipping because it is involved in oncogenesis by suppressing c‐Cbl binding and impairing MET degradation [3].
Case reports on the efficacy of crizotinib therapy in patients harboring the MET Y1003 point mutation exist [4, 5], but none on the efficacy of tepotinib or capmatinib, more selective MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Herein, we report the use of tepotinib in a patient with advanced lung adenocarcinoma harboring the MET Y1003N point mutation.
2. Case Report
A 63‐year‐old woman with no smoking history was referred to our hospital with a chief complaint of left‐sided chest pain for 2 months. A computed tomography of the trunk revealed a 36‐mm mass in the upper lobe of the left lung, left‐sided pleural effusion, and bone metastases in the lumbar vertebra and sacrum. Transbronchial lung biopsy confirmed adenocarcinoma (Figure 1), resulting in cT4N1M1c stage IVB lung adenocarcinoma diagnosis.
Figure 2 shows the patient's treatment course. The patient received two cycles of cisplatin, pemetrexed, and pembrolizumab. After first‐line therapy, next‐generation sequencing on a pleural fluid cellblock using FoundationOne CDx (Foundation Medicine, Cambridge, MA) detected the MET Y1003N point mutation. As MET inhibitors are not approved for use against this mutation in Japan, the patient subsequently received treatment with nab‐paclitaxel, S‐1, and docetaxel/ramucirumab. After review and approval by our institution's drug safety department and after obtaining patient consent, capmatinib (400 mg twice daily) was initiated as fifth‐line therapy. However, on day 22 of treatment, the patient showed a grade 3 alanine transaminase (ALT) increase (188 U/L), Grade 2 aspartate transaminase (AST, 126 U/L) and total bilirubin increase (2.6 mg/dL), leukopenia (2000/μL), and thrombocytopenia (67 000/μL), and capmatinib was discontinued before efficacy confirmation. Chest radiography at the end of capmatinib treatment showed a decrease in left pleural effusion but no reduction in the mass in the left upper lung field. Before and after capmatinib treatment, the carcinoembryonic antigen level decreased from 5.9 to 5.5 ng/mL (< 5.0), whereas the sialyl Lewis‐x antigen level increased from 34.6 to 38.6 U/mL (< 38). Thereafter, nab‐paclitaxel and gemcitabine were sequentially administered. One year and 11 months after diagnosis, tepotinib (500 mg once daily) was started as eighth‐line treatment with patient consent and department approval. Tumors decreased in size after tepotinib initiation (−30.9%), with a partial response (PR) after 5 months of treatment (Figure 3). Tepotinib was discontinued after 8 months because of confirmed tumor recurrence. During tepotinib treatment, Grade 1 AST and ALT increases were observed as adverse events. After tepotinib discontinuation, the patient received vinorelbine, which did not yield a positive response, and chemotherapy was terminated. The patient died 3 years after treatment initiation.
3. Discussion
Herein, we present a case of advanced lung adenocarcinoma in a patient harboring the MET Y1003N mutation who responded to tepotinib for 8 months after seven prior chemotherapy regimens. To our best knowledge, this is the first report on the use of selective type 1b MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors capmatinib or tepotinib in a patient harboring the MET Y1003 mutation. Two case studies reported the effectiveness of crizotinib, a multikinase inhibitor, as first‐line therapy in attaining a PR. One patient responded for 10 months [4], whereas the other responded for > 8 months, while having recorded pulmonary thromboembolism and liver function abnormalities at treatment initiation [5]. Tepotinib's efficacy in lung adenocarcinoma with MET ex14 skipping was reportedly favorable compared to crizotinib's efficacy [6], and it is currently one of the standard treatments for this lung cancer type. Furthermore, tepotinib is reportedly effective regardless of the line of treatment and is expected to be effective in heavily pretreated patients [7]. Therefore, selective type 1b MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as tepotinib may be a preferred treatment option for MET Y1003 point mutations compared to crizotinib.
MET Y1003 mutation is a rare driver oncogene; detected in 0.06% (4/7140) of lung adenocarcinomas and 0.17% (2/1206) of lung squamous cell carcinomas [8]. Y1003 is contained in the c‐MET juxtamembrane domain encoded in MET ex14 and is the binding site for the c‐Cbl E3 ubiquitin ligase. The binding of c‐Cbl to Y1003 causes the MET receptor to be incorporated into endosomes, ubiquitinated, and degraded. Similar to MET ex14 skipping, mutations in Y1003 result in MET receptor overexpression through this degradation abnormality, leading to carcinogenesis [9]. In vitro, cell lines with the Y1003F mutation as well as MET ex14 skipping mutation exhibit activation of downstream signaling pathways such as extracellular signal‐regulated kinase and AKT phosphorylation as well as induction of motility and migration upon hepatocyte growth factor stimulation [10]. These responses can be suppressed by capmatinib in both mutations; thus, selective type 1b MET tyrosine kinase inhibitor may be an effective treatment option.
In conclusion, a patient with heavily pretreated lung adenocarcinoma harboring the MET Y1003N mutation responded to tepotinib treatment for 8 months. Targeted therapy should be used upfront; however, selective type 1b MET tyrosine kinase inhibitors may be a treatment option, even for patients who have received multiple prior treatment regimens.
